title: Part 4, Chapter 1
paragraphs: "Can this still be a dream?" Raskolnikov thought once more.
He studied the unexpected visitor carefully and suspiciously.
"Svidrigaïlov! Nonsense! It can't be!" he said at last, aloud, in bewilderment.
The visitor didn't seem at all surprised by this exclamation.

"I've come to you for two reasons. First, I wanted to make your personal acquaintance, as I've already heard a great deal about you that's interesting and flattering. Second, I hope you won't refuse to help me in a matter directly concerning the welfare of your sister, Avdotya Romanovna. Without your support, she probably wouldn't let me anywhere near her now, given her prejudice against me. But with your help, I expect—"
"You expect wrong," Raskolnikov interrupted.
"They only arrived yesterday, may I ask?"
Raskolnikov gave no reply.

"It was yesterday, I know. I arrived the day before myself. Well, let me say this, Rodion Romanovitch: I don't consider it necessary to justify myself, but kindly tell me—what was so particularly criminal about my behaviour in all this, speaking without prejudice, with common sense?"
Raskolnikov continued to stare at him in silence.

"That in my own house I persecuted a defenseless girl and 'insulted her with my infamous proposals'—is that it? I'm getting ahead of you, I know. But just suppose that I, too, am a man, et nihil humanum—in a word, that I'm capable of being attracted and falling in love, which is something that doesn't depend on our will. Then everything can be explained in the most natural way. The question is: am I a monster, or am I myself a victim? And what if I am a victim? When I proposed to the object of my passion that we elope to America or Switzerland, I may have felt the deepest respect for her and believed I was promoting our mutual happiness! Reason is the slave of passion, you know. Perhaps I was doing more harm to myself than anyone!"

"But that's not the point," Raskolnikov interrupted with disgust. "Quite simply, whether you're right or wrong, we find you repellent. We want nothing to do with you. We're showing you the door. Get out!"
Svidrigaïlov broke into a sudden laugh.
"There's no getting around you, is there?" he said, laughing in the frankest way. "I hoped to get around you, but you went straight to the heart of it!"
"But you're still trying to get around me!"

"What of it?" Svidrigaïlov cried, laughing openly. "It's what the French call bonne guerre—the most innocent form of deception! But you interrupted me. One way or another, I repeat: there would never have been any unpleasantness if it weren't for what happened in the garden. Marfa Petrovna—"
"You got rid of Marfa Petrovna too, from what they say," Raskolnikov cut in rudely.

"Oh, so you've heard that as well? Naturally. As for your question, I really don't know what to say, though my conscience is perfectly clear on that score. Don't think I'm worried about it. Everything was proper and in order. The medical inquiry diagnosed apoplexy from bathing immediately after a heavy dinner with a bottle of wine, and it couldn't have found anything else. But I'll tell you what I've been thinking about lately, especially on my way here in the train: did I perhaps contribute to the whole catastrophe—morally, somehow, by irritating her or something? But I concluded that was quite impossible too."
Raskolnikov laughed.
"I'm surprised you even bother about it!"

"But what are you laughing at? Consider—I only struck her twice with a switch, and there weren't even any marks. Don't think me a cynic, please. I'm perfectly aware how vile that was and so on. But I also know for certain that Marfa Petrovna was actually rather pleased by my, shall we say, ardor. The scandal over your sister had been squeezed dry; for three days Marfa Petrovna had been stuck at home with nothing to show off in town. And then those two switches fell from heaven! Her very first act was to order the carriage harnessed! Not to mention the fact that there are cases when women are very, very glad to be insulted, whatever indignation they may show. Everyone is like that, in fact; human beings in general love to be insulted—have you noticed? But it's especially true of women. You might almost say it's their only entertainment."
For a moment Raskolnikov thought of getting up and leaving, ending the conversation. But something—a kind of curiosity, even a certain prudence—held him back.
"You enjoy fighting?" he asked carelessly.

"No, not particularly," Svidrigaïlov answered calmly. "Marfa Petrovna and I hardly ever fought. We lived very harmoniously and she was always pleased with me. I only used the whip twice in all our seven years—not counting a third occasion that was rather ambiguous. The first time was two months after our wedding, right after we arrived in the country, and the last was the one we're discussing. You thought I was some kind of monster, a reactionary, a slave driver? Ha ha! By the way, do you remember, Rodion Romanovitch, how a few years ago, in those days of 'beneficent publicity,' a nobleman—I've forgotten his name—was put to shame everywhere, in all the papers, for thrashing a German woman on the train? Remember? It was around that same time, that very year I think, that the 'disgraceful affair of the Age' took place—you know, 'The Egyptian Nights,' that public reading? The dark eyes! Ah, the golden days of youth, where are they? Well, as for the gentleman who thrashed the German, I feel no sympathy for him—after all, why would I? But I must say that sometimes you encounter such provocative 'Germans' that I doubt any progressive could entirely vouch for himself. No one looked at it from that angle then, but it's the truly humane point of view, I assure you."
After saying this, Svidrigaïlov burst into sudden laughter again. Raskolnikov could see clearly that this was a man with a firm purpose in mind, well able to keep it to himself.
"I take it you haven't talked to anyone for several days?" he asked.
"Hardly anyone. I suppose you're wondering how I can be so adaptable?"
"No, I'm wondering why you're too adaptable."

"Because I'm not offended by the rudeness of your questions? Is that it? But why take offense? You asked, and I answered," he replied with a surprising expression of simplicity. "You know, there's hardly anything that interests me," he went on, as though dreamily, "especially now. I've nothing to do. You're perfectly free to think I'm courting you with an ulterior motive, especially since I told you I want to see your sister about something. But I'll confess frankly—I'm terribly bored. These last three days especially, so I'm delighted to have you. Don't be angry, Rodion Romanovitch, but you seem somehow terribly strange yourself. Say what you like, but there's something wrong with you, and now too—not this very minute, I mean, but in general. Well, well, I won't push it. Don't scowl! I'm not such a boor as you think."
Raskolnikov looked at him gloomily.
"You're perhaps not a boor at all," he said. "In fact, I rather think you're a man of good breeding, or at least know how to behave like one on occasion."

"I'm not particularly interested in anyone's opinion," Svidrigaïlov answered drily, with a shade of haughtiness. "So why not be vulgar when it suits? Vulgarity makes such a convenient disguise in our climate—especially if one has a natural inclination that way," he added, laughing again.
"But I've heard you have plenty of connections here. You're, as they say, 'not without resources.' So what do you want with me, unless you have some special purpose?"

"That's true, I do have friends here," Svidrigaïlov admitted, ignoring the main point. "I've already seen some of them. I've been knocking about for three days and either I've seen them or they've seen me. That's natural enough. I'm well dressed, not considered poor. The emancipation of the serfs didn't affect me—my property consists mainly of forests and water meadows, so the income hasn't dropped. But I'm not going to visit them; I was sick of them long ago. I've been here three days without calling on a single one. What a city this is! How did it come into being? A city of officials and students of every stripe. Yes, there's a great deal I didn't notice eight years ago, when I was running wild here. My only hope now is in anatomy, by God!"
"Anatomy?"
"But as for those clubs, the Dussauts, the promenades, so-called progress—well, it can all get along without me," he continued, ignoring the question again. "Besides, who wants to be a cardsharp?"
"You were a cardsharp, then?"

"How could I not be? There was a regular set of us, all men of the best society, eight years ago. We had a fine time. And all men of breeding, you know—poets, men of property. And actually, as a rule in Russian society, the best manners are found among those who've been thrashed. Have you noticed? I've gone downhill in the country. Still, I did land in debtors' prison, thanks to a shady Greek from Nezhin. Then Marfa Petrovna turned up, haggled with him, and bought me out for thirty thousand silver. I owed seventy thousand in all. We were united in lawful matrimony, and she spirited me off to the country like a treasure. She was five years older than me, you know. She was very fond of me. For seven years I never left the estate. And note this: my entire life, she held a document over me—that IOU for thirty thousand—so if I ever stirred up trouble, I'd be trapped immediately. And she would have done it! Women see no contradiction in that sort of thing."
"And if it hadn't been for that, would you have bolted?"

"I don't know what to say. It was hardly the document that held me. I didn't want to go anywhere. Marfa Petrovna herself suggested a trip abroad when she saw I was bored, but I'd been abroad before and it always made me feel wretched. For no reason—you look at the sunrise, the Bay of Naples, the sea, and it makes you sad. What's most revolting is that you're genuinely sad! No, it's better at home. At least here you can blame others for everything and make excuses for yourself. I might have gone on an expedition to the North Pole—j'ai le vin mauvais, I can't stand drinking, and there's nothing left but drink. I've tried it. But tell me—I've heard Berg is going up in a great balloon next Sunday from the Yusupov Garden and will take passengers for a fee. Is it true?"
"Would you go up?"
"I—no, not really," Svidrigaïlov muttered, seeming genuinely lost in thought.
"What does he mean? Is he serious?" Raskolnikov wondered.

"No, the document didn't hold me back," Svidrigaïlov went on reflectively. "It was my own doing, staying put. And nearly a year ago, Marfa Petrovna gave me back the document on my name day and threw in a considerable sum of money besides. She had a fortune, you know. 'See how I trust you, Arkady Ivanovitch'—those were her exact words. You don't believe she actually said that? But, you know, I managed the estate quite decently. They know me in the district. I ordered books, too. Marfa Petrovna approved at first, but then worried I was overstudiying."
"You seem to miss Marfa Petrovna a great deal."
"Miss her? Perhaps. Really, perhaps I do. And by the way, do you believe in ghosts?"
"What ghosts?"
"Ordinary ghosts."
"Do you?"
"Perhaps not, pour vous plaire. I wouldn't say no exactly."
"Do you see them, then?"
Svidrigaïlov looked at him rather oddly.
"Marfa Petrovna is kind enough to visit me," he said, twisting his mouth into a strange smile.
"What do you mean, 'kind enough to visit'?"

"She's come three times. I first saw her on the day of the funeral itself, an hour after the burial. It was the day before I left for here. The second time was the day before yesterday, at dawn, at the Malaya Vishera station, on the journey. The third was two hours ago, in the room where I'm staying. I was alone."
"Were you awake?"
"Fully awake. Wide awake every time. She comes, talks to me for a minute, and goes out the door—always the door. I can almost hear her."
"What made me think something like this must be happening to you?" Raskolnikov said suddenly.
At the same moment he was surprised at having said it. He was greatly agitated.
"Really? You thought that?" Svidrigaïlov asked in astonishment. "Did you really? Didn't I say there was something in common between us?"
"You never said that!" Raskolnikov cried sharply and with heat.
"Didn't I?"
"No!"
"I thought I did. When I came in and saw you lying with your eyes shut, pretending, I said to myself at once: 'Here's the man.'"
"What do you mean, 'the man'? What are you talking about?" Raskolnikov cried.
"What do I mean? I really don't know," Svidrigaïlov muttered artlessly, as though he too were puzzled.
For a minute they were silent, staring at each other.
"That's all nonsense!" Raskolnikov shouted in irritation. "What does she say when she comes to you?"

"She? Would you believe it—she talks about the most trivial things, and it makes me angry. Man is a strange creature. The first time she came—I was tired, you know: the funeral service, the burial, the luncheon afterward; finally I was left alone in my study, I lit a cigar and started thinking—she came in through the door. 'You've been so busy today, Arkady Ivanovitch, you forgot to wind the dining-room clock,' she said. I'd wound that clock every week for seven years, and whenever I forgot, she'd always remind me. The next day I was on my way here. I got out at the station at daybreak after sleeping badly, eyes half open, drinking some coffee—and there was Marfa Petrovna suddenly sitting beside me with a pack of cards. 'Shall I tell your fortune for the journey, Arkady Ivanovitch?' She was a great hand at fortune-telling. I'll never forgive myself for not letting her. I ran off in fright, and besides, the bell rang. Then today, sitting in my room after a miserable dinner from a cook-shop, smoking—suddenly Marfa Petrovna again. She came in all dressed up, in a new green silk dress with a long train. 'Good day, Arkady Ivanovitch! How do you like my dress? Aniska can't make like this.' Aniska was a dressmaker in the country, one of our former serf girls who'd trained in Moscow—a pretty thing. She stood there turning in front of me. I looked at the dress, then looked carefully at her face. 'I wonder you trouble to come to me about such trifles, Marfa Petrovna.' 'Good gracious, you won't let one bother you about anything!' To tease her, I said: 'I want to get married, Marfa Petrovna.' 'That's just like you, Arkady Ivanovitch. It doesn't do you much credit to come looking for a bride when you've barely buried your wife. And if you could make a good choice! But I know it won't be for your happiness or hers—you'll only be a laughingstock to everyone.' Then she went out, and her train seemed to rustle. Isn't that nonsense?"
"But perhaps you're lying?" Raskolnikov put in.
"I rarely lie," Svidrigaïlov answered thoughtfully, apparently not noticing the rudeness of the question.
"And before this—had you ever seen ghosts?"

"Y-yes, once in my life, six years ago. I had a serf named Filka. Just after his burial, I called out, forgetting: 'Filka, my pipe!' He came in and went to the cupboard where my pipes were. I sat still and thought: 'He's doing it out of revenge,' because we'd had a violent quarrel just before his death. 'How dare you come in with a hole in your elbow,' I said. 'Get out, you wretch!' He turned and left, and never came again. I didn't tell Marfa Petrovna at the time. I wanted to have a memorial service said for him, but I was ashamed."
"You should see a doctor."

"I know I'm not well without your telling me, though I don't know exactly what's wrong. I'm probably five times as strong as you. I didn't ask whether you believe ghosts can be seen—I asked whether you believe they exist."
"No, I refuse to believe it!" Raskolnikov cried with genuine anger.

"What do people usually say?" Svidrigaïlov murmured, as though talking to himself, looking aside and tilting his head. "They say: 'You're ill, so what you see is only unreal fantasy.' But that's not strictly logical. I agree that ghosts only appear to the sick, but that only proves they can't appear to anyone but the sick—not that they don't exist."
"Of course they don't!" Raskolnikov insisted irritably.

"No? You don't think so?" Svidrigaïlov went on, looking at him steadily. "But what about this argument—help me with it: ghosts are, as it were, shreds and fragments of other worlds, the beginnings of them. A healthy person naturally has no reason to see them, because he is above all a creature of this earth and must, for the sake of wholeness and order, live only in this life. But the moment one falls ill, the moment the normal earthly order of the organism breaks down, one begins to sense the possibility of another world. And the more seriously ill one becomes, the closer the contact with that other world, so that at the moment of death one steps directly into it. I thought about this a long time ago. If you believe in a future life, you could believe this too."
"I don't believe in a future life," said Raskolnikov.
Svidrigaïlov sat lost in thought.
"And what if there are only spiders there, or something of that sort?" he said suddenly.
"He's a madman," thought Raskolnikov.

"We always imagine eternity as something beyond our comprehension, something vast, enormous! But why must it be vast? What if instead of all that, it's just one little room—like a bathhouse in the country, blackened with soot, with spiders in every corner—and that's all eternity is? I sometimes picture it that way."
"Can you really imagine nothing more just and comforting than that?" Raskolnikov cried, with a feeling of anguish.
"More just? Who knows—perhaps that is just. And you know, it's exactly what I would have made it," Svidrigaïlov answered with a vague smile.
This horrible answer sent a cold shiver through Raskolnikov. Svidrigaïlov raised his head, looked at him, and suddenly burst out laughing.

"Just think!" he cried. "Half an hour ago we'd never laid eyes on each other. We considered ourselves enemies. There's an unsettled matter between us. We've tossed it aside and gone sailing off into abstractions! Wasn't I right when I said we were birds of a feather?"
"Allow me," Raskolnikov went on irritably, "to ask you to explain why you've honored me with your visit—and I'm in a hurry, I have no time to waste. I want to go out."
"By all means. Your sister, Avdotya Romanovna, is going to marry Mr. Luzhin, Pyotr Petrovitch?"
"Can you refrain from any question about my sister, from even mentioning her name? I can't understand how you dare utter her name in my presence, if you really are Svidrigaïlov."
"But I've come here precisely to talk about her. How can I avoid mentioning her?"
"Very well. Speak, but be quick."

"I'm sure you've already formed your own opinion of this Mr. Luzhin, a connection of mine through my wife, if you've spent even half an hour with him or heard any facts about him. He's no match for Avdotya Romanovna. I believe she is sacrificing herself, generously and rashly, for the sake of her family. From everything I'd heard about you, I thought you'd be very glad if the match could be broken off without any loss of practical advantage. Now that I know you personally, I'm convinced of it."
"All this is very naïve—excuse me, I should say impudent—on your part," said Raskolnikov.

"You mean I'm pursuing my own interests. Don't worry, Rodion Romanovitch—if I were acting from self-interest, I wouldn't have spoken so openly. I'm not a complete fool. I'll confess something psychologically curious: just now, defending my love for Avdotya Romanovna, I called myself the victim. Well, let me tell you that I feel no love for her now, not the slightest, so that I'm surprised at myself, because I really did feel something—"
"From idleness and depravity," Raskolnikov put in.
"I'm certainly idle and depraved. But your sister has qualities that even I couldn't help being struck by. But that's all nonsense, as I now see."
"Have you seen that for long?"

"I began to be aware of it some time ago, but became fully certain only the day before yesterday, almost at the moment I arrived in Petersburg. In Moscow, though, I still fancied I was coming to win Avdotya Romanovna's hand and cut out Mr. Luzhin."
"Excuse me for interrupting, but please be brief and come to the point. I'm in a hurry, I want to go out."

"With pleasure. On arriving here and deciding on a certain journey, I'd like to make some necessary preliminary arrangements. I left my children with an aunt; they're well provided for and have no need of me personally. And what kind of father would I make? I took only what Marfa Petrovna gave me a year ago. That's enough for me. Forgive me—I'm getting to the point. Before this journey, which may or may not happen, I want to settle the matter of Mr. Luzhin too. It's not that I especially detest him, but it was through him that I quarreled with Marfa Petrovna when I found out she'd cooked up this marriage. I now want to see Avdotya Romanovna through your mediation, and if you like, in your presence, to explain first that she'll gain nothing but harm from Mr. Luzhin. Then, begging her pardon for all past unpleasantness, to offer her a gift of ten thousand roubles and thus help bring about the break with Mr. Luzhin—a break which I believe she herself would welcome, if she could see a way to it."
"You really are mad!" cried Raskolnikov, more astonished than angry. "How dare you talk like that!"

"I knew you'd protest. But first, though I'm not rich, this ten thousand is entirely free. I have absolutely no need of it. If Avdotya Romanovna won't accept it, I'll waste it on something far more foolish. Second, my conscience is perfectly clear—I make the offer with no hidden motive. You may not believe me, but in time both Avdotya Romanovna and you will understand. The point is that I did cause your sister, whom I deeply respect, some trouble and unhappiness, and so, sincerely regretting it, I want—not to compensate or repay her, but simply to do something for her benefit, to show that I'm not privileged to do nothing but harm. If my offer had even the smallest trace of self-interest, I wouldn't have made it so openly, and I wouldn't be offering only ten thousand when five weeks ago I offered more. Besides, I may very soon marry a young lady, which should dispel any suspicion of designs on Avdotya Romanovna. In conclusion, let me point out that in marrying Mr. Luzhin, she'd be taking money just the same—only from a different man. Don't be angry, Rodion Romanovitch. Think it over calmly."
Svidrigaïlov himself was exceedingly calm and composed as he said all this.
"I beg you to say no more," said Raskolnikov. "In any case, this is unpardonable impudence."

"Not at all. Then a man may do nothing but harm in this world, and is prevented from doing the smallest bit of good by trivial social conventions. That's absurd. If I died and left this sum to your sister in my will, surely she wouldn't refuse it?"
"Very likely she would."
"Oh, come. Well, if you refuse, so be it, though ten thousand roubles can be a very useful thing to have. In any case, I ask you to pass on what I've said to Avdotya Romanovna."
"No, I won't."
"In that case, Rodion Romanovitch, I'll be forced to seek a meeting with her myself, which would mean troubling her."
"And if I do pass it on, will you not try to see her?"
"I really don't know what to say. I would very much like to see her once."
"Don't count on it."
"I'm sorry. But you don't know me. Perhaps we'll become better acquainted."
"You think we might?"

"And why not?" Svidrigaïlov said with a smile. He stood up and took his hat. "I didn't really mean to disturb you, and I came without expecting much, though I was very struck by your face this morning."
"Where did you see me this morning?" Raskolnikov asked uneasily.

"I saw you by chance. I kept thinking there's something about you that's like me. But don't worry—I'm not pushy. I got along well with cardsharps; I never bored Prince Svirbey, a great personage and a distant relative; I could write about Raphael's Madonna in Madame Prilukov's album; I never left Marfa Petrovna's side for seven years; and I used to stay at Viazemsky's house in the Haymarket in the old days. And perhaps I'll go up in the balloon with Berg."
"Very well. Are you setting off on your travels soon, may I ask?"
"What travels?"
"Why, that 'journey' you mentioned."

"A journey? Oh yes, I did mention a journey. Well, that's a broad subject. If only you knew what you're asking," he added, and gave a sudden, short laugh. "Perhaps I'll get married instead of traveling. They're arranging a match for me."
"Here?"
"Yes."
"How have you had time for that?"

"But I'm very anxious for an interview with Avdotya Romanovna. I beg you earnestly. Well, goodbye for now. Oh yes! I nearly forgot something. Tell your sister, Rodion Romanovitch, that Marfa Petrovna remembered her in her will and left her three thousand roubles. That's absolutely certain. She arranged it a week before her death, in my presence. Avdotya Romanovna should be able to collect the money in two or three weeks."
"Are you telling the truth?"
"Yes. Tell her. Well, at your service. I'm staying very close to you."
As he went out, Svidrigaïlov bumped into Razumihin in the doorway.
